advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: What does the term 'cosmid' stand for?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: Cosmid is derived from 'cos' (cohesive end sites of lambda phage) + 'plasmid'. It is a hybrid vector combining a plasmid backbone (with ori and antibiotic resistance) and lambda cos sites (for in vitro packaging), developed by Collins and Hohn in 1978.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: காஸ்மிடு என்பது 'cos' (லாம்டா பாஜின் ஒட்டும் முனை இடங்கள்) + 'பிளாஸ்மிடு' என்பதிலிருந்து வந்தது. இது பிளாஸ்மிடு முதுகெலும்பையும் (ori, நுண்ணுயிர்க்கொல்லி எதிர்ப்புடன்) லாம்டா cos இடங்களையும் (உடலகத்துக்கு வெளியே பொதிவுக்கு) இணைக்கும் கலப்பினத் தாங்கிக்கடத்தி; 1978-இல் காலின்ஸும் ஹோனும் உருவாக்கினர்.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: What is the insert capacity of a cosmid vector?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: Cosmids can accept 35–45 kb of foreign DNA. This is because lambda phage heads package DNA between 37–52 kb in size between two cos sites. The small cosmid backbone (~5–6 kb) leaves 35–45 kb available for insert DNA.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: காஸ்மிடுகள் 35–45 kb அயல் DNA-வை ஏற்கும். ஏனெனில் லாம்டா பாஜ் தலைகள் இரு cos இடங்களுக்கிடையே 37–52 kb அளவுள்ள DNA-வைப் பொதிக்கும். சிறிய காஸ்மிடு முதுகெலும்பு (~5–6 kb) உட்செருகு DNA-வுக்கு 35–45 kb இடத்தை விட்டுவைக்கிறது.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: Which three structural elements are absolutely essential for a functional YAC?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: A functional YAC requires: TEL (telomeres) to protect linear chromosome ends, CEN (centromere) for accurate chromosome segregation during cell division, and ARS (Autonomously Replicating Sequence — origin of replication in yeast) to allow replication once per cell cycle.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: செயல்படும் YAC-க்கு முற்றிலும் அவசியமான மூன்று கட்டமைப்புக் கூறுகள் எவை?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: செயல்படும் YAC-க்குத் தேவை: நேரியல் நிறமூர்த்த முனைகளைப் பாதுகாக்க TEL (டீலோமியர்கள்); செல் பிரிவில் நிறமூர்த்தங்களைச் சரியாகப் பிரிக்க CEN (சென்ட்ரோமியர்); செல் சுழற்சிக்கு ஒருமுறை இரட்டிப்பாக ARS (தன்னிச்சையாக இரட்டிப்பாகும் வரிசை — ஈஸ்டில் இரட்டிப்பு தொடக்கம்).

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: What is the approximate insert capacity of a Yeast Artificial Chromosome (YAC)?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: YACs can accept 200 kb to 2,000 kb (2 Mb) of foreign DNA — far larger than any other standard cloning vector. This enormous capacity made YACs essential tools in the Human Genome Project for mapping and sequencing large chromosomal regions.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: ஈஸ்ட் செயற்கை நிறமூர்த்தத்தின் (YAC) தோராய உட்செருகு கொள்ளளவு என்ன?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: YAC-கள் 200 kb முதல் 2,000 kb (2 Mb) வரை அயல் DNA-வை ஏற்கும் — எந்தப் பிற நிலையான குளோனிங் தாங்கிக்கடத்தியையும்விட மிகப் பெரியது. இதனால் பெரிய நிறமூர்த்தப் பகுதிகளை வரைபடமாக்கவும் வரிசையாக்கவும் மனித மரபணுத்தொகைய திட்டத்தில் YAC-கள் இன்றியமையாதவையாயின.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: SV40 (Simian Virus 40) has a genome size of approximately:
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: The SV40 genome is approximately 5,243 bp of circular double-stranded DNA. This small size limits its insert capacity to ~2.5 kb as a cloning vector, since the total packaged DNA must fit within the viral capsid (maximum ~5.2 kb).
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: SV40 மரபணுத்தொகை தோராயமாக 5,243 bp வட்ட இரட்டை இழை DNA. பொதிக்கப்படும் மொத்த DNA வைரஸ் கேப்சிடுக்குள் (அதிகபட்சம் ~5.2 kb) பொருந்த வேண்டியிருப்பதால், தாங்கிக்கடத்தியாக இதன் உட்செருகு கொள்ளளவு ~2.5 kb ஆகக் குறைகிறது.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: What is the primary function of the Large T antigen (LT-Ag) of SV40?
o: Encode viral capsid proteins VP1, VP2, VP3
Package viral DNA into the capsid
Transfer viral DNA into the nucleus of the host cell
Initiate viral DNA replication by binding to the SV40 ori and transform host cells
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: SV40 Large T antigen (LT-Ag) has two main functions: (1) It binds to the SV40 origin of replication (ori) to initiate and drive viral DNA replication; (2) It inhibits host tumor suppressors p53 and Rb, causing cell transformation. LT-Ag expressed in COS cells allows SV40 vectors to replicate to very high copy numbers.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: SV40-இன் பெரிய T எதிர்ப்பொருளின் (LT-Ag) முதன்மைச் செயல் என்ன?
o_ta: வைரஸ் கேப்சிடு புரதங்கள் VP1, VP2, VP3-ஐக் குறியீடு செய்தல்
வைரஸ் DNA-வை விருந்தோம்பி செல்லின் உட்கருவுக்குள் கடத்துதல்
SV40 ori-யுடன் இணைந்து வைரஸ் DNA இரட்டிப்பைத் தொடங்குதலும் விருந்தோம்பி செல்களை உருமாற்றுதலும்
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: SV40 பெரிய T எதிர்ப்பொருளுக்கு (LT-Ag) இரு முக்கியச் செயல்கள்: (1) SV40 இரட்டிப்பு தொடக்கத்துடன் (ori) இணைந்து வைரஸ் DNA இரட்டிப்பைத் தொடங்கி இயக்குகிறது; (2) விருந்தோம்பியின் கட்டி அடக்கிகளான p53, Rb-ஐத் தடுத்து செல் உருமாற்றத்தை ஏற்படுத்துகிறது. COS செல்களில் வெளிப்படுத்தப்படும் LT-Ag, SV40 தாங்கிக்கடத்திகளை மிக உயர்ந்த படி எண்ணிக்கைக்கு இரட்டிப்பாக்க உதவுகிறது.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: Who discovered transposons ('jumping genes') and in which organism?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: Transposons were discovered by Barbara McClintock in Zea mays (maize) in the 1940s. She observed that certain genetic elements could move between chromosomal positions, causing changes in kernel color patterns. She was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1983 for this discovery.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: இடம்பெயர் மரபணுக்களை ('தாவும் மரபணுக்கள்') கண்டுபிடித்தவர் யார், எந்த உயிரினத்தில்?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: இடம்பெயர் மரபணுக்களை 1940-களில் பார்பரா மெக்ளின்டாக் Zea mays (மக்காச்சோளம்)-இல் கண்டுபிடித்தார். சில மரபணு உறுப்புகள் நிறமூர்த்த இடங்களுக்கிடையே நகர்ந்து, தானிய நிற அமைப்புகளை மாற்றுவதை அவர் கண்டார். இக்கண்டுபிடிப்புக்காக 1983-இல் உடலியல் அல்லது மருத்துவத்துக்கான நோபல் பரிசு பெற்றார்.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: Which of the following is the key enzyme that mediates the cut-and-paste movement of DNA transposons?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: Transposase is the enzyme encoded within Class II (DNA) transposons that mediates transposition. It recognizes and binds to the Terminal Inverted Repeats (TIRs) at both ends of the transposon, excises it from the donor site, and catalyzes its integration at a new target site.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: DNA இடம்பெயர் மரபணுக்களின் வெட்டி-ஒட்டும் இயக்கத்தை நடுவணாற்றும் முக்கிய நொதி எது?
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: டிரான்ஸ்போசேஸ் என்பது வகுப்பு II (DNA) இடம்பெயர் மரபணுக்களுக்குள் குறியீடு செய்யப்படும் நொதி; இடம்பெயர்வை நடுவணாற்றுகிறது. இது இடம்பெயர் மரபணுவின் இரு முனைகளிலுமுள்ள முனை தலைகீழ் மீள்வரிசைகளை (TIR) அடையாளம் கண்டு இணைந்து, அதைக் கொடையாளி இடத்திலிருந்து வெட்டி, புதிய இலக்கு இடத்தில் ஒருங்கிணைப்பைத் தூண்டுகிறது.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: COS cells are used in SV40-based expression systems because they:
o: Stably express SV40 Large T antigen, enabling high-copy episomal replication of SV40 ori-containing vectors
Are derived from human embryonic kidney cells
Produce lambda phage capsid proteins for packaging
Have a YAC integrated into their chromosomes
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: COS cells (e.g., COS-1, COS-7) are African green monkey kidney (CV-1) cells that stably express the SV40 Large T antigen. When SV40 vectors containing the viral ori are transfected into COS cells, the T antigen drives high-level episomal replication, producing thousands of copies of the vector per cell and enabling very high transient gene expression.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: SV40 அடிப்படை வெளிப்பாட்டு அமைப்புகளில் COS செல்கள் பயன்படுத்தப்படுவது ஏனெனில் அவை:
o_ta: SV40 பெரிய T எதிர்ப்பொருளை நிலையாக வெளிப்படுத்தி, SV40 ori கொண்ட தாங்கிக்கடத்திகளின் உயர்படி எபிசோம் இரட்டிப்பை இயலச்செய்கின்றன
பொதிவுக்கான லாம்டா பாஜ் கேப்சிடு புரதங்களை உருவாக்குகின்றன
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: COS செல்கள் (எ.கா. COS-1, COS-7) SV40 பெரிய T எதிர்ப்பொருளை நிலையாக வெளிப்படுத்தும் ஆப்பிரிக்கப் பச்சைக் குரங்கின் சிறுநீரக (CV-1) செல்கள். வைரஸ் ori கொண்ட SV40 தாங்கிக்கடத்திகள் COS செல்களுள் கடத்தப்படும்போது, T எதிர்ப்பொருள் உயர்மட்ட எபிசோம் இரட்டிப்பை இயக்கி, ஒரு செல்லுக்கு ஆயிரக்கணக்கான தாங்கிக்கடத்திப் படிகளை உருவாக்கி, மிக உயர்ந்த தற்காலிக மரபணு வெளிப்பாட்டை இயலச்செய்கிறது.

advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q: Which of the following correctly ranks cloning vectors by their insert capacity from smallest to largest?
o: Cosmid < Lambda phage < Plasmid < YAC < SV40
Lambda phage < Cosmid < Plasmid < SV40 < YAC
SV40 < Plasmid < Lambda phage < Cosmid < YAC
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e: From smallest to largest insert capacity: SV40 (~2.5 kb) < Plasmid (up to ~10 kb) < Lambda phage replacement vectors (~23 kb) < Cosmid (35–45 kb) < YAC (200–2,000 kb). YACs have by far the largest capacity. Note that SV40 is smaller than standard plasmids due to the capsid size constraint.
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.q_ta: உட்செருகு கொள்ளளவின்படி குளோனிங் தாங்கிக்கடத்திகளைச் சிறியதிலிருந்து பெரியதாக எது சரியாக வரிசைப்படுத்துகிறது?
o_ta: காஸ்மிடு < லாம்டா பாஜ் < பிளாஸ்மிடு < YAC < SV40
லாம்டா பாஜ் < காஸ்மிடு < பிளாஸ்மிடு < SV40 < YAC
SV40 < பிளாஸ்மிடு < லாம்டா பாஜ் < காஸ்மிடு < YAC
advanced_vectors_cosmid_yac_sv40_transpo.e_ta: சிறியதிலிருந்து பெரிய உட்செருகு கொள்ளளவு: SV40 (~2.5 kb) < பிளாஸ்மிடு (~10 kb வரை) < லாம்டா பாஜ் பதிலீட்டுத் தாங்கிக்கடத்திகள் (~23 kb) < காஸ்மிடு (35–45 kb) < YAC (200–2,000 kb). YAC-களுக்கே மிகப் பெரிய கொள்ளளவு. கேப்சிடு அளவுக் கட்டுப்பாட்டால் SV40 நிலையான பிளாஸ்மிடுகளைவிடச் சிறியது என்பதைக் கவனிக்க.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: In the colour code of biotechnology, red biotechnology refers to:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: Red = medical; green = agricultural; white = industrial; blue = marine.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q_ta: உயிரித் தொழில்நுட்பவியலின் வண்ணக் குறியீட்டில் சிவப்பு உயிரித் தொழில்நுட்பவியல் குறிப்பது:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: சிவப்பு = மருத்துவம்; பச்சை = வேளாண்மை; வெள்ளை = தொழிற்சாலை; நீலம் = கடல்.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: The enzyme that seals nicks between adjacent nucleotides in the DNA backbone is:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q_ta: DNA முதுகெலும்பிலுள்ள அடுத்தடுத்த நியுக்ளியோடைடுகளுக்கிடையேயான வெட்டுகளை அடைக்கும் நொதி:

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: In pBR322, insertion of DNA at the BamHI site gives the phenotype:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: BamHI lies in tet, so tet is inactivated; amp is intact.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q_ta: pBR322-இல் BamHI இடத்தில் DNA செருகப்பட்டால் கிடைக்கும் பண்பு:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: BamHI tet-க்குள் உள்ளதால் tet செயலிழக்கிறது; amp அப்படியே உள்ளது.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: The T-DNA of the Ti plasmid is flanked by:
o: Left and right 25 bp border repeats
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: T-DNA lies between the LB and RB border repeats.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: T-DNA, LB மற்றும் RB எல்லை மீள்வரிசைகளுக்கிடையே அமைந்துள்ளது.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: High cI represses lytic genes; RecA activation (SOS) later cleaves cI and induces the prophage.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: அதிக cI சிதைவுச் சுழற்சி மரபணுக்களை அடக்கும்; பின்னர் RecA செயல்பாடு (SOS) cI-ஐப் பிளந்து புரோபாஜைத் தூண்டும்.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: Its ssDNA form serves as a template for Sanger sequencing and mutagenesis.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: இதன் ssDNA வடிவம் சாங்கர் வரிசையாக்கத்துக்கும் திடீர்மாற்ற உருவாக்கத்துக்கும் வார்ப்புருவாகப் பயன்படுகிறது.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: A cosmid is a hybrid of:
o: Plasmid and cos sites of lambda
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: Plasmid replication plus lambda cos sites for packaging.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: பிளாஸ்மிடு இரட்டிப்பும் பொதிவுக்கான லாம்டா cos இடங்களும்.

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: Which vector can carry the largest foreign DNA?
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q_ta: மிகப் பெரிய அயல் DNA-வைச் சுமக்கக்கூடிய தாங்கிக்கடத்தி எது?

atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q: A genomic library differs from a cDNA library in that it contains:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e: Genomic libraries include introns and regulatory DNA.
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.q_ta: மரபணுத்தொகைய நூலகம் cDNA நூலகத்திலிருந்து வேறுபடுவது அது கொண்டிருப்பதில்:
atlas1_fundamentals_vectors.html.e_ta: மரபணுத்தொகைய நூலகங்களில் இன்ட்ரான்களும் ஒழுங்குபடுத்தும் DNA-வும் உள்ளன.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: Which step comes immediately after ligation in gene cloning?
atlas2_techniques.html.e: Ligated DNA is introduced into the host (transformation) before selection and screening.
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: மரபணுக் குளோனிங்கில் இணைப்புக்கு உடனடியாக அடுத்து வரும் படி எது?
atlas2_techniques.html.e_ta: இணைக்கப்பட்ட DNA, தேர்வு, சலிக்கைக்கு முன் விருந்தோம்பிக்குள் (உருமாற்றம்) செலுத்தப்படுகிறது.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: Heat-shock transformation of E. coli typically uses:
atlas2_techniques.html.e: CaCl₂-treated cells receive a brief heat shock at 42 °C.
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: E. coli-யின் வெப்ப அதிர்ச்சி உருமாற்றத்தில் வழக்கமாகப் பயன்படுவது:
atlas2_techniques.html.e_ta: CaCl₂ சிகிச்சை பெற்ற செல்கள் 42 °C-இல் சிறிய வெப்ப அதிர்ச்சியைப் பெறுகின்றன.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: Delivery of DNA by a virus is called:
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: வைரஸ் மூலம் DNA செலுத்தப்படுவது எவ்வாறு அழைக்கப்படுகிறது?

atlas2_techniques.html.q: In replica plating after insertional inactivation of tet, a recombinant colony will:
o: Grow on amp and on amp + tet
atlas2_techniques.html.e: The insert disrupts tet: it grows on ampicillin but not on tetracycline.
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: tet-இல் உட்செருகல் செயலிழப்புக்குப் பின் நகல் வளர்ப்பில், மறுசேர்க்கைக் காலனி:
atlas2_techniques.html.e_ta: உட்செருகு tet-ஐ சிதைக்கிறது: ஆம்பிசிலினில் வளரும், டெட்ராசைக்ளினில் வளராது.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: In blue-white screening a recombinant colony is:
atlas2_techniques.html.e: Insert disrupts lacZα, so X-gal is not cleaved: white.
atlas2_techniques.html.e_ta: உட்செருகு lacZα-ஐ சிதைப்பதால் X-gal பிளக்கப்படுவதில்லை: வெள்ளை.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: IPTG in blue-white plates acts as:
o: A gratuitous inducer of the lac promoter
atlas2_techniques.html.e: IPTG is a non-metabolisable inducer; X-gal is the chromogenic substrate.
atlas2_techniques.html.e_ta: IPTG வளர்சிதைமாற்றமாகாத தூண்டி; X-gal நிறம் தரும் வினைபடு பொருள்.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: In Sanger sequencing, chain termination occurs because ddNTPs lack:
atlas2_techniques.html.e: Without a 3′-OH no phosphodiester bond can form.
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: சாங்கர் வரிசையாக்கத்தில் ddNTP-களில் இல்லாததால் சங்கிலி முடிவுறுகிறது:

atlas2_techniques.html.q: After 30 cycles of ideal PCR, one template copy yields about:
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: இலட்சிய PCR-இன் 30 சுழற்சிகளுக்குப் பின் ஒரு வார்ப்புருப் படி தோராயமாகத் தருவது:

atlas2_techniques.html.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis DNA moves towards the:
atlas2_techniques.html.e: DNA is negatively charged and migrates to the anode (+).
atlas2_techniques.html.q_ta: அகரோஸ் ஜெல் மின்னொட்டத்தில் DNA நகர்வது எதை நோக்கி?
atlas2_techniques.html.e_ta: DNA எதிர்மின்னூட்டம் கொண்டதால் நேர்மின்வாயை (+) நோக்கி நகரும்.

atlas2_techniques.html.q: Which blot detects proteins with antibodies?

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: In pronuclear microinjection the transgene is injected into the:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: The larger male pronucleus is usually injected.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: Positive-negative selection in gene targeting uses:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: neo (G418) selects integration; tk (ganciclovir) kills random integrants.
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e_ta: neo (G418) ஒருங்கிணைப்பைத் தேர்ந்தெடுக்கும்; tk (கான்சிக்ளோவிர்) தற்போக்கு ஒருங்கிணைப்புகளைக் கொல்லும்.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: Offspring of two heterozygous knockout mice are knockout (−/−) in what proportion?
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q_ta: ஹெட்டிரோசைகஸ் மரபணு நீக்க எலிகள் இரண்டின் (+/−) சந்ததிகளில் மரபணு நீக்கம் (−/−) கொண்டவை எவ்வளவு விகிதத்தில்?

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: Dolly was produced by transferring a nucleus from:
o: An udder (mammary) cell of an adult ewe
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: Nucleus from a mammary gland cell of a 6-year-old ewe.
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e_ta: 6 வயது பெண் செம்மறியின் பாலூட்டிச் சுரப்பி செல்லிலிருந்து உட்கரு.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: HAT medium kills unfused myeloma cells because they lack:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: Aminopterin blocks de novo synthesis; HGPRT-deficient myeloma cannot use the salvage pathway.
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q_ta: இணையாத மைலோமா செல்களை HAT ஊடகம் கொல்வது அவற்றிடம் இல்லாததால்:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e_ta: அமினோப்டெரின் புதிதாக்கத் தொகுப்பைத் தடுக்கும்; HGPRT குறைபாடுள்ள மைலோமா மீட்புப் பாதையைப் பயன்படுத்த இயலாது.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: A monoclonal antibody whose name ends in -zumab is:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e_ta: -omab எலி வகை; -ximab கலப்புரு; -zumab மனிதமயமாக்கப்பட்டது; -umab மனித வகை.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: The first successful human gene therapy trial (1990) treated:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: ADA-SCID, an ex vivo T-cell therapy.
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q_ta: முதல் வெற்றிகரமான மனித மரபணு சிகிச்சைச் சோதனை (1990) சிகிச்சையளித்த நோய்:

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: The NGG PAM sits just 3′ of the protospacer.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q: Error-prone repair of a Cas9 double-strand break by NHEJ typically causes:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: NHEJ leaves indels that often knock out the gene.
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.q_ta: Cas9 இரட்டை இழை முறிவை NHEJ பிழை-வாய்ப்புள்ள முறையில் பழுதுபார்ப்பது வழக்கமாக ஏற்படுத்துவது:
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e_ta: NHEJ இண்டெல்களை விட்டுச்செல்லும்; இவை பெரும்பாலும் மரபணுவை நீக்கிவிடும்.

o: Based on restriction sites with probes
atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e: RAPD gives dominant markers using arbitrary 10-mer primers.

atlas3_transgenic_medical.html.e_ta: RAPD, தற்போக்கு 10-மர பிரைமர்களைப் பயன்படுத்தி ஓங்கு குறிப்பான்களைத் தருகிறது.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: Animal cells in culture are normally grown at:
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: 37 °C with 5% CO₂ maintains pH with a bicarbonate buffer.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: Phenol red in the medium indicates:
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: It turns yellow when acidic and purple when alkaline.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: Cells should be subcultured during which phase?
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Subculture in the log phase, at 70–80% confluence.

o: Finite divisions of normal diploid cells (~50)
The size limit of a bioreactor
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Normal cells divide about 40–60 times before senescence.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: Which cell line is used most widely for recombinant protein production?
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: CHO cells produce most therapeutic mAbs.
Four factors reprogram somatic cells to iPSCs.

o: All three germ layers but not the whole organism
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Pluripotent: any body cell type; totipotent: also extraembryonic tissue.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: A bioreactor suited to shear-sensitive cells is:
o: Rushton-turbine stirred tank at high rpm
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Airlift has no impeller and gives gentle mixing.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: In ethanol fermentation, the enzyme converting acetaldehyde to ethanol is:
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Alcohol dehydrogenase uses NADH and regenerates NAD⁺.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: Which describes the Celera approach to the human genome?
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Celera used whole-genome shotgun; the public project used hierarchical BAC mapping.

atlas4_culture_society.html.q: In India a patent lasts for:
atlas4_culture_society.html.e: Twenty years from the filing date.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.q: Which three databases form the INSDC?
atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: GenBank (USA), ENA (Europe) and DDBJ (Japan) exchange data daily.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.q: A FASTA header line begins with:

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: Swiss-Prot is the reviewed part of UniProtKB; TrEMBL is unreviewed.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.q: Which algorithm gives an optimal global alignment?
atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: Needleman–Wunsch (1970) is global; Smith–Waterman is local.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.q: In a dot plot, a long diagonal line indicates:
atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: Diagonals mark similar segments; off-diagonals mark repeats.

o: Translated nucleotide query to a protein database
atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: BLASTX translates the query in six frames and searches proteins.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.q: Which E-value suggests the most significant match?

o: Substitution matrix built from conserved blocks
atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: BLOSUM62 uses blocks clustered at 62% identity.
The Protein Data Bank archives 3-D coordinates.

atlas5_bioinformatics.html.q: The most common experimental method in the PDB is:

o: The most closely related pair according to the guide tree
atlas5_bioinformatics.html.e: It follows the guide tree from closest to most distant.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: What does the term 'bioinformatics' refer to?
o: The study of microorganisms using microscopes
The application of computer science and mathematics to store, retrieve, and analyse biological data
The use of living organisms to manufacture industrial products
The study of protein three-dimensional structures only
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: Bioinformatics is the interdisciplinary science that applies computer science, mathematics, and statistics to acquire, store, organise, analyse, and interpret biological data — especially large-scale molecular sequence data.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: Which of the following is a PRIMARY nucleotide sequence database?
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: GenBank is a primary nucleotide sequence database — it stores original, experimentally determined DNA and RNA sequences submitted directly by researchers. UniProt, KEGG, and Pfam are secondary or derived databases.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: GenBank is maintained by which organisation?
o: National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), NIH
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: GenBank is maintained by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), which is part of the National Institutes of Health (NIH) in the United States.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: Which is the OLDEST nucleotide sequence database?
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: The EMBL Nucleotide Sequence Database was established in 1980 — two years before GenBank (1982) and six years before DDBJ (1986), making it the oldest of the three INSDC nucleotide databases.

o: International Network for Sequence Data Collection
International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration — the partnership between GenBank, EMBL, and DDBJ
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: INSDC stands for International Nucleotide Sequence Database Collaboration — the formal partnership between GenBank (USA), EMBL/ENA (Europe), and DDBJ (Japan) for daily synchronisation and sharing of all nucleotide sequence records.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: Within how many hours does INSDC synchronise a newly submitted sequence across all three databases?
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: Under the INSDC agreement, a sequence submitted to any one of the three databases (GenBank, EMBL, DDBJ) is shared with and available in the other two within 24 hours of submission.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: The DDBJ database is maintained in which country?
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: DDBJ (DNA Data Bank of Japan) is maintained by the National Institute of Genetics (NIG) in Mishima, Shizuoka, Japan. It is the Asian hub of the INSDC.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: Which search tool is primarily associated with EMBL nucleotide database searches?
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: SRS (Sequence Retrieval System) is the search tool primarily associated with the EMBL/ENA database at the European Bioinformatics Institute. GenBank uses Entrez; DDBJ uses Sakura.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: What is an 'accession number' in the context of nucleotide databases?
o: A unique permanent identifier assigned to each deposited sequence record
A password for accessing the database
The number of nucleotides in a sequence
The year the sequence was deposited
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: An accession number (e.g., AY123456) is a unique, permanent identifier assigned to each sequence record when it is deposited in an INSDC database. It never changes and allows unambiguous citation and retrieval of any specific sequence globally.

bioinformatics_databases_app.html.q: Which bioinformatics tool is used to compare a query DNA sequence against all sequences in GenBank to find similar sequences?
bioinformatics_databases_app.html.e: BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool) compares a user-submitted query sequence against all sequences in the GenBank database and returns similar sequences ranked by statistical significance (E-value). It is the most widely used bioinformatics tool globally.

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.e: Needleman–Wunsch (1970) gives a global pairwise alignment.

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.q: In Smith–Waterman local alignment, negative scores in the matrix are:
bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.e: Scores are floored at zero, so alignments can start anywhere.

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.q: Which substitution matrix is the default for BLASTP?

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.e: Sequences are homologous or not; identity and similarity are measurable percentages.

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.q: Which BLAST program compares a translated nucleotide query with a protein database?

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.e: Smaller E-value = fewer chance matches expected.

bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.q: The usual strategy of Clustal for multiple alignment is:
o: Exact dynamic programming in N dimensions
Progressive alignment guided by a tree
bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.e: Clustal builds a guide tree and aligns progressively.

o: Visualise, analyse and model protein structures
bioinformatics_tools_alignment_blast.htm.e: It is a molecular graphics and modelling tool.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: Who coined the term 'Biotechnology' and in which year?
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ The term Biotechnology was coined by Hungarian engineer Károly Ereky in 1919 to describe large-scale pig production using sugar beets as feed.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: Which of the following is the correct UN CBD (1992) definition of biotechnology?
o: The use of computers to analyse biological data
The cultivation of microorganisms in industrial bioreactors
Any technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives to make or modify products
The study of genes and heredity in living organisms
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ The UN Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) defines biotechnology as any technological application that uses biological systems, living organisms, or derivatives to make or modify products or processes for specific use.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: What is the colour code for Agricultural Biotechnology?
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Green Biotechnology refers to agricultural applications — GM crops, Bt cotton, tissue culture, biofertilisers. Red = Medical, White = Industrial, Blue = Marine.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: The first recombinant human insulin (Humulin) was commercially produced using:
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Human insulin (Humulin) was first produced commercially in 1982 by Eli Lilly using Escherichia coli with the recombinant human insulin gene. This was the first commercially successful rDNA product.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: Which enzyme acts as 'molecular scissors' in recombinant DNA technology?
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) act as 'molecular scissors' — they cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences. DNA ligase acts as 'molecular glue' to join fragments.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: Bt cotton contains the 'cry' gene derived from:
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Bt cotton contains the cry gene from Bacillus thuringiensis. This gene encodes Cry proteins (Bt toxin) that are toxic to bollworm larvae but harmless to mammals. Bt cotton was approved in India in 2002.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) was invented by:
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Kary Mullis invented PCR in 1983 and received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993. PCR amplifies specific DNA sequences in vitro using thermal cycling and Taq DNA polymerase from Thermus aquaticus.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: Monoclonal antibody technology (hybridoma technique) was developed by:
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Georges Köhler and César Milstein developed hybridoma technology in 1975, earning the Nobel Prize in 1984. The technique fuses B lymphocytes with myeloma cells to produce monoclonal antibodies.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: Which of the following is a correct example of bioremediation?
o: Using UV radiation to sterilise water
Using Pseudomonas putida to degrade petroleum hydrocarbons in oil spills
Using nitrogen fertilisers to improve crop yield
Using restriction enzymes to cut DNA
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Bioremediation uses microorganisms to degrade pollutants. Pseudomonas putida (first GMO patented by A. M. Chakrabarty, 1980) can degrade multiple petroleum hydrocarbons and is used in oil spill clean-up.

biotechnology_fundamentals.html.q: CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing technology received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in:
biotechnology_fundamentals.html.e: ✅ Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020 for developing CRISPR-Cas9 as a precise genome editing tool, described as 'a tool for rewriting the code of life.'

blotting_techniques.html.q: The blotting technique used to detect a specific DNA sequence is called:
blotting_techniques.html.e: Southern blotting detects DNA; it is named after Edwin Southern (1975).

blotting_techniques.html.q: Northern blotting is used to detect:
blotting_techniques.html.e: Northern blotting detects RNA and shows gene expression and transcript size.

blotting_techniques.html.q: In a Western blot, proteins are first separated by:
blotting_techniques.html.e: Proteins are separated by SDS-PAGE and then electroblotted onto a membrane.

blotting_techniques.html.q: Why is the gel treated with NaOH in Southern blotting?
o: To convert double-stranded DNA to single strands
blotting_techniques.html.e: Alkali denatures DNA so single strands bind the membrane and can hybridise with the probe.

blotting_techniques.html.q: Northern blot gels contain formaldehyde in order to:
o: Prevent secondary structure so RNA migrates by size
blotting_techniques.html.e: Formaldehyde keeps RNA unfolded, so migration reflects length.

blotting_techniques.html.q: The enzyme commonly linked to the secondary antibody in a Western blot is:
blotting_techniques.html.e: HRP (or alkaline phosphatase) catalyses the reaction that produces a signal.

blotting_techniques.html.q: The purpose of the blocking step is to:
o: Cover free sites and reduce background
blotting_techniques.html.e: Blocking agents (milk, BSA, Denhardt's) occupy unused binding sites and lower background.

blotting_techniques.html.q: Transfer of DNA in a classical Southern blot is driven by:
blotting_techniques.html.e: Buffer drawn upward by a stack of paper towels carries DNA to the membrane: capillary transfer.

blotting_techniques.html.q: Which membrane is commonly used in Western blotting?
blotting_techniques.html.e: PVDF and nitrocellulose bind proteins well.

blotting_techniques.html.q: To check whether a transgene has integrated into the genome of a transgenic animal, the best blot is:
blotting_techniques.html.e: Southern blotting shows presence, copy number and integration pattern of DNA.

o: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Controlled RNA Insertion System for Precise Regulation
Cloning and Replication of Integrated Short Palindromic RNA
Cascade RNA Interference System for Protein Repair
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats — sequences found in bacterial genomes as part of their immune system.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: What is the natural function of CRISPR in bacteria?
o: To help bacteria divide more rapidly
To act as an adaptive immune system against viral infection
To produce antibiotics against competing bacteria
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: CRISPR is the bacterial adaptive immune system. It stores viral DNA sequences as spacers, and on re-infection, uses them to guide Cas proteins to cut and destroy viral DNA.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: Which enzyme acts as the 'molecular scissors' in CRISPR gene editing?
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: Cas9 (CRISPR-Associated Protein 9) is the nuclease enzyme that creates a double-strand break in DNA at the site directed by the guide RNA.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: What is the function of the guide RNA (gRNA) in CRISPR-Cas9?
o: To cut the DNA at the target site
To repair the DNA after cutting
To direct Cas9 to the specific target DNA sequence
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: The gRNA (~20 nucleotides) is complementary to the target DNA sequence and acts as a molecular GPS, guiding Cas9 to the precise location in the genome.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: What is the PAM sequence recognised by SpCas9?
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: The PAM sequence for Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) is 5′-NGG-3′ (where N = any nucleotide). This sequence must be present adjacent to the target site for Cas9 to bind and cut.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: NHEJ (Non-Homologous End Joining) repair after a CRISPR cut typically results in:
o: Random insertions or deletions (indels), causing gene disruption
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: NHEJ is an error-prone repair pathway that randomly rejoins the broken DNA ends, introducing small insertions or deletions (indels) — typically causing a frameshift mutation that disrupts gene function (knockout).

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: Which DNA repair pathway is used for precise gene correction when a donor template is provided?
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: HDR (Homology-Directed Repair) uses a provided donor DNA template to repair the cut site with precision — enabling gene correction or insertion of a new sequence.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: In 2023, the first approved CRISPR-based gene therapy (Casgevy) was developed for which disease?
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: Casgevy was approved by the UK MHRA and US FDA in 2023 for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassaemia, marking the first approved CRISPR-based human therapy.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 for CRISPR-Cas9 was awarded to:
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: Jennifer Doudna (UC Berkeley) and Emmanuelle Charpentier (Max Planck Institute) received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing CRISPR-Cas9 as a precision gene-editing tool.

crispr_gene_editing_app.html.q: Why is CRISPR germline editing considered more ethically concerning than somatic editing?
o: Germline editing produces heritable changes affecting all future generations
Germline editing is less efficient than somatic editing
Germline editing costs more than somatic editing
Germline editing affects only the treated patient
crispr_gene_editing_app.html.e: Germline editing modifies eggs, sperm, or embryos — making the genetic changes heritable. Every future descendant of the edited individual will carry the change, raising profound ethical concerns about consent and unintended consequences.

o: A collection of cloned DNA fragments in vectors maintained in host cells representing the genome of a source organism
A digital database of DNA sequences stored on computers
A collection of purified DNA enzymes used in genetic engineering
A physical building where DNA samples are stored at low temperatures
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: A DNA library is a collection of cloned DNA fragments, each carried in a vector and maintained in a population of host cells (usually E. coli). Together, the clones represent all or most of the genetic information of the source organism.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: What is the primary source of DNA for constructing a genomic DNA library?
o: mRNA isolated from a specific tissue
Total genomic DNA from any nucleated cell
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: A genomic DNA library is constructed from total genomic DNA isolated from any nucleated cell of the organism. All cells contain the same genomic DNA regardless of tissue type.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: Which enzyme is central to the construction of a cDNA library?
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: Reverse transcriptase (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase) is the key enzyme in cDNA library construction. It synthesises complementary DNA (cDNA) from mRNA templates, allowing expressed genes to be captured as DNA.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: Why is a cDNA library tissue-specific while a genomic library is not?
o: Because cDNA libraries use different restriction enzymes in different tissues
Because genomic DNA is different in different cell types
Because vectors used for cDNA libraries can only survive in certain tissues
Because cDNA is derived from mRNA, which reflects only the genes actively expressed in that specific tissue or condition
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: A cDNA library is built from mRNA, which represents only the genes being actively transcribed in a specific tissue at a specific time. Different tissues express different sets of genes. Genomic DNA is identical in all cells of an organism.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: What is the function of oligo-dT cellulose chromatography in cDNA library construction?
o: To fragment genomic DNA into small pieces
To selectively purify poly-A mRNA from total RNA
To amplify the cDNA by PCR
To ligate cDNA into the vector
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: Oligo-dT cellulose columns selectively bind the poly-A tail of eukaryotic mRNA through complementary base pairing (A-T). rRNA and tRNA, which lack poly-A tails, pass through the column unbound, allowing purification of mRNA.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: Why does a cDNA library NOT contain introns?
o: Because introns are removed by restriction enzymes before cloning
Because reverse transcriptase cannot copy intron sequences
Because only coding sequences are present in genomic DNA
Because cDNA is made from processed mRNA from which introns have already been spliced out
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: mRNA is the result of transcription followed by RNA processing (splicing), which removes introns. cDNA is made by copying this processed mRNA, so it contains only exon sequences — no introns are present in cDNA.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: What is the correct order of steps in cDNA synthesis?
o: DNA isolation → restriction digestion → ligation → transformation
mRNA isolation → PCR amplification → gel electrophoresis → sequencing
mRNA isolation → first-strand cDNA synthesis → mRNA removal → second-strand synthesis → ligation into vector
Genomic DNA isolation → restriction digestion → packaging → infection of E. coli
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: cDNA synthesis proceeds: (1) mRNA isolation (oligo-dT purification); (2) First-strand synthesis by reverse transcriptase (oligo-dT primer + RT → mRNA:cDNA hybrid); (3) mRNA removal by RNase H; (4) Second-strand synthesis by DNA Polymerase I; (5) Ligation into vector and transformation.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: Which vector would be most appropriate for constructing a genomic library of a large organism like humans?
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: The human genome is ~3.2 Gb. YACs can accept 200–2,000 kb of DNA, making them ideal for constructing complete genomic libraries of large genomes. Standard plasmids (<10 kb) and lambda phage (~23 kb) would require millions of clones each.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: What does the Clarke-Carbon formula calculate?
o: The molecular weight of a DNA fragment
The number of clones needed to represent the complete genome in a library with a given probability
The number of restriction enzyme sites in a genome
The efficiency of transformation of E. coli
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: The Clarke-Carbon formula N = ln(1−P) / ln(1−f) calculates the minimum number of clones (N) required to achieve a probability (P, usually 0.99) of finding any given sequence in a genomic library, where f is the fractional size of each insert relative to the total genome.

dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.q: A researcher wants to produce human insulin using bacteria. Which library would be most appropriate to use as the source of the insulin gene?
o: A cDNA library prepared from human pancreatic beta cells
A lambda phage genomic library from human liver
dna_library_genomic_cdna.html.e: A cDNA library from pancreatic beta cells (which highly express insulin) is ideal. The insulin cDNA lacks introns — bacteria cannot splice introns. The genomic insulin gene contains introns and cannot be correctly expressed in E. coli. This is exactly how recombinant human insulin was produced (approved 1982).

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: Which of the following enzymes is called a 'molecular scissor' in genetic engineering?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: Restriction endonucleases are called molecular scissors because they cut DNA at specific palindromic sequences with extreme precision, just as scissors cut paper at a defined point.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: EcoRI recognizes the sequence 5'-GAATTC-3'. What type of ends does it produce after cleavage?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: EcoRI makes a staggered cut between G and A on each strand, producing 5' overhangs (single-stranded -AATT tails). These are called 5' sticky ends or cohesive ends.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: Which restriction enzyme produces blunt ends?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: SmaI cuts 5'-GGG-CCC-3' at the center of its palindromic recognition sequence, producing fully double-stranded blunt ends with no single-stranded overhangs.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: DNA ligase catalyzes the formation of which type of bond to join two DNA fragments?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: DNA ligase catalyzes formation of a covalent 3'-5' phosphodiester bond between the 3'-OH of one fragment and the 5'-phosphate of the adjacent fragment, sealing nicks in the DNA backbone.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: Reverse transcriptase is used to synthesize which molecule?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: Reverse transcriptase, found in retroviruses, catalyzes synthesis of complementary DNA (cDNA) using single-stranded mRNA as a template, reversing the normal direction of genetic information flow.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: Taq polymerase is isolated from which source organism?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: Taq polymerase is isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a thermophilic bacterium found in hot springs. Its thermostability at up to 95°C makes it ideal for use in PCR.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: What is the primary purpose of treating a vector with alkaline phosphatase before cloning?
o: To create sticky ends on the vector
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: Alkaline phosphatase removes 5'-phosphate groups from linearized vector ends. Without these phosphates, the vector cannot self-ligate, forcing incorporation of insert DNA and improving cloning efficiency.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: Which Nobel Prize was awarded to Arber, Smith, and Nathans for the discovery of restriction enzymes?
o: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1978
Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1975
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: Werner Arber, Hamilton Smith, and Daniel Nathans were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1978 for the discovery and application of restriction endonucleases.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: A palindromic DNA sequence is best described as:
o: A sequence that codes for multiple proteins
A sequence where both strands read identically in the 5' to 3' direction
A sequence with the same nucleotide at all positions
A sequence that is present only in viral genomes
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: A palindromic DNA sequence reads identically on both strands in the 5' to 3' direction. For example, GAATTC reads the same on both strands when each is read 5' to 3'. This symmetry is what restriction enzymes recognize.

enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.q: Which of the following enzymes is essential for the extension step in PCR?
enzymes_genetic_engineering.html.e: Taq polymerase is the thermostable DNA polymerase used in PCR. During the extension step at approximately 72°C, it synthesizes new DNA strands from annealed primers using the denatured template, amplifying the target sequence.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: Why does DNA migrate towards the anode (positive electrode) in gel electrophoresis?
o: DNA has positive charge due to its sugar backbone
DNA is negatively charged due to phosphate groups in the backbone and therefore migrates towards the positive electrode
DNA is neutral but is physically pushed by the buffer flow
DNA contains positive nitrogen atoms that attract to the anode
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: DNA carries a net negative charge at neutral pH because of the phosphate groups in its backbone. Negatively charged molecules always migrate towards the positive electrode (anode) in an electric field. This consistent negative charge means all DNA fragments have the same charge-to-mass ratio, so separation is based on SIZE (molecular sieving) rather than charge differences between fragments.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: In agarose gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragment migrates the FURTHEST from the loading well?
o: All fragments migrate the same distance
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: Smaller DNA fragments pass through gel pores more easily than larger ones (molecular sieving). A 500 bp fragment migrates far more efficiently than a 10,000 bp or 5,000 bp fragment in the same time. This is the fundamental principle — smaller = faster = farther from the well.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: What is the mathematical relationship between DNA fragment size and migration distance in gel electrophoresis?
o: Log of fragment size is inversely proportional to migration distance (logarithmic relationship)
Fragment size is directly proportional to migration distance (linear relationship)
Fragment size is proportional to the square root of migration distance
There is no predictable relationship between size and migration distance
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: The relationship is logarithmic: log(fragment size in bp) is inversely proportional to migration distance. When log(bp) is plotted against migration distance on a graph, a straight line results. This standard curve from the DNA ladder allows accurate interpolation of unknown fragment sizes.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: What is the PRIMARY function of glycerol in the DNA loading dye?
o: It increases the density of the sample so it sinks into the well and does not float away into the buffer
It stains the DNA to make it visible under UV light
It speeds up DNA migration through the gel
It prevents the DNA from degrading in the well
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: Glycerol (or Ficoll) in the loading dye increases the density of the DNA sample. This ensures the sample sinks to the bottom of the well when loaded and does not diffuse upward into the surrounding buffer. The tracking dyes (bromophenol blue and xylene cyanol) in the loading dye provide visible colour to monitor migration progress.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: Ethidium bromide (EtBr) is added to agarose gels to:
o: Increase the migration speed of DNA fragments
Maintain the pH of the gel during electrophoresis
Prevent non-specific binding of DNA to the gel matrix
Intercalate into DNA and produce orange fluorescence under UV light for band visualisation
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: Ethidium bromide intercalates (inserts) between the base pairs of DNA. When illuminated with UV light (302 nm), EtBr-DNA complexes fluoresce bright orange, making the DNA bands visible. EtBr is a sensitive stain — detecting as little as 1–10 ng DNA per band. However, it is a potent mutagen and carcinogen requiring strict safety precautions.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: In SDS-PAGE, the role of SDS (sodium dodecyl sulphate) is to:
o: Increase the pore size of the polyacrylamide gel
Stain the protein bands for visualisation
Provide the ionic strength needed for electrophoresis
Denature proteins and coat them with uniform negative charge so separation is based only on molecular weight
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: SDS is an anionic detergent that binds to proteins proportional to their chain length. This coating of uniform negative charge eliminates differences in the native charge and shape of proteins, ensuring all proteins have the same charge-to-mass ratio. Separation in SDS-PAGE is therefore purely by molecular weight — unlike native PAGE which also depends on shape and intrinsic charge.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: What is the main purpose of the DNA ladder loaded in gel electrophoresis?
o: To provide an energy source for DNA migration
To stain all DNA bands uniformly for comparison
To provide reference migration distances for known fragment sizes, enabling unknown sizes to be estimated
To prevent DNA degradation during electrophoresis
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: A DNA ladder contains fragments of precisely known sizes (e.g., 100 bp, 500 bp, 1 kb…). By measuring the migration distance of each ladder band and plotting log(bp) vs distance, a standard curve (straight line) is generated. Unknown sample band sizes are estimated by measuring their migration distances and interpolating from this standard curve.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: Why is a 3% agarose gel used instead of a 0.5% gel when analysing PCR products in the 100–500 bp range?
o: 3% agarose is cheaper and easier to prepare
3% agarose conducts electricity better at low voltages
Higher agarose concentration creates smaller pores, providing better resolution of small DNA fragments
Higher concentration gels run faster, saving time
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: Increasing agarose concentration reduces the average pore size of the gel matrix. Smaller pores provide greater retardation to small DNA fragments, improving their separation. A 3% gel is ideal for resolving small fragments (50–500 bp). Conversely, a 0.5% gel has large pores better suited for separating large fragments (5–50 kb) with low resistance to their movement.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: Where are the DNA samples loaded in agarose gel electrophoresis, and why?
o: At the anode (+) end, so DNA migrates away towards the cathode
At the cathode (−) end, so the negatively charged DNA migrates towards the anode across the gel
In the middle of the gel for equidistant migration to both electrodes
Anywhere on the gel surface — position does not matter
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: DNA samples are loaded into wells at the CATHODE (−) end of the gel. Since DNA is negatively charged, it migrates away from the negative electrode (repulsion) and towards the positive electrode (anode). Loading at the cathode end provides the maximum migration path through the entire gel to the anode, achieving maximum separation of different-sized fragments.

gel_electrophoresis.html.q: A researcher runs an agarose gel and observes a smeared band instead of a sharp discrete band. What is the most likely cause?
o: The voltage was too low, causing insufficient separation
The gel percentage was too high for the fragment sizes
The DNA ladder was loaded in the wrong well
The DNA sample was degraded (DNase contamination) or the well was overloaded
gel_electrophoresis.html.e: Band smearing typically indicates DNA degradation — partial degradation by DNase contamination produces a continuous distribution of fragment sizes instead of a discrete band at one position. Overloading the well with too much DNA can also cause smearing. Solutions: ensure all materials are RNase/DNase-free; reduce DNA loading amount; check sample for intact bands before electrophoresis.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: What is the correct definition of gene cloning?
o: Asexual reproduction of an entire organism
Sequencing the entire genome of an organism
Production of multiple identical copies of a specific gene using recombinant DNA technology
Amplifying a gene using the polymerase chain reaction only
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: Gene cloning is the process of producing multiple identical copies of a specific gene by inserting it into a vector, introducing the recombinant vector into a host cell, and allowing the host to replicate — copying the gene with each cell division.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: Why must the same restriction enzyme be used to cut both the insert DNA and the vector?
o: To cut DNA into smaller, more manageable fragments
To ensure both molecules have complementary (compatible) sticky ends for ligation
Because restriction enzymes only work on foreign DNA
To prevent the host cell from degrading the recombinant DNA
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: Using the same restriction enzyme on both insert and vector generates identical sticky end sequences on both molecules. These complementary overhangs can anneal by hydrogen bonding, positioning the ends correctly for DNA ligase to seal them covalently.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: T4 DNA ligase is used in gene cloning to:
o: Cut DNA at specific restriction sites
Amplify the gene of interest by PCR
Form phosphodiester bonds between the insert and vector DNA ends
Introduce recombinant DNA into the host cell
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: T4 DNA ligase catalyses the formation of covalent phosphodiester bonds between the 3'-OH of one DNA strand and the 5'-phosphate of the adjacent strand. It 'seals' the nick between the insert and vector, creating a continuous circular recombinant DNA molecule.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: In blue-white screening, white colonies indicate:
o: Recombinant clones where the insert has disrupted the lacZ gene
Cells where the lacZ gene is intact and functional
Cells that have died from antibiotic exposure
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: White colonies contain an insert cloned into the MCS within the lacZ gene. This disrupts lacZ, so no functional β-galactosidase is produced. X-gal in the medium is not cleaved — no blue compound forms — so the colony appears white. White = recombinant.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: In blue-white screening, the purpose of adding X-gal to the medium is:
o: To provide a colourless substrate that β-galactosidase cleaves to produce a blue product
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: X-gal (5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-β-D-galactopyranoside) is a colourless substrate. When β-galactosidase (encoded by an intact lacZ gene) cleaves X-gal, it releases a blue compound (5-bromo-4-chloro-indigo), turning the colony blue.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: In insertional inactivation using pBR322, when the gene of interest is cloned into the BamHI site (within tet^r), the recombinant cell will be:
o: Sensitive to both ampicillin and tetracycline
Resistant to both ampicillin and tetracycline
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: The insert disrupts the tet^r gene (tetracycline resistance), making the cell tetracycline-sensitive. The amp^r gene is not affected, so the cell remains ampicillin-resistant. Recombinants grow on ampicillin but NOT on tetracycline; identified by replica plating.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: Which method is used to introduce recombinant plasmid DNA into competent E. coli cells?
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: Transformation is the process of introducing naked DNA into competent bacterial cells. Two main methods: (1) Chemical — CaCl₂ treatment to make cells competent, followed by brief heat shock at 42°C. (2) Electroporation — a high-voltage electric pulse creates temporary pores for DNA entry.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: What is the main purpose of alkaline phosphatase treatment of the linearised vector before ligation?
o: To fragment the vector into smaller pieces
To add phosphate groups to the vector ends for better ligation
To remove 5'-phosphate groups from vector ends, preventing self-ligation and reducing non-recombinant background
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: Alkaline phosphatase removes the 5'-phosphate groups from the linearised vector ends. Without these groups, the vector cannot self-ligate (cannot re-circularise on its own). This forces the vector to ligate only with insert DNA (which retains its 5'-phosphates), greatly reducing the background of non-recombinant clones.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: After transformation, bacterial cells are first plated on ampicillin-containing medium. This step specifically selects for:
o: Cells that contain the recombinant vector with the correct insert
All transformed cells (those that took up the vector, with or without insert)
Cells that have undergone recombination of their chromosomal DNA
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: Plating on ampicillin selects for cells carrying the vector (which has the amp^r gene). Both recombinant (vector + insert) and non-recombinant (re-ligated vector only) cells survive. Non-transformed cells (no vector) die. A second step (blue-white or insertional inactivation) is then needed to distinguish recombinant from non-recombinant transformants.

gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.q: Which of the following is the correct sequence of steps in gene cloning?
o: Isolation of gene → Restriction digestion → Ligation → Transformation → Selection and screening
gene_cloning_steps_selection.html.e: The correct sequence is: (1) Isolate gene of interest; (2) Restriction digestion of gene and vector with same enzyme; (3) Ligation (insert + vector) using T4 DNA ligase; (4) Transformation into competent E. coli; (5) Selection on antibiotic medium (transformants); (6) Screening for recombinants (blue-white / insertional inactivation).

o: Introduction of therapeutic genes into patient cells to treat disease
Cloning of genes in bacteria for study
Modification of crop genes for higher yield
gene_therapy_app.html.e: Gene therapy introduces therapeutic genes into a patient's cells to correct or compensate for a defective gene.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: In ex vivo gene therapy, the gene transfer takes place:
o: Outside the patient's body in a laboratory
gene_therapy_app.html.e: Ex vivo (outside the living) gene therapy involves removing cells, modifying them in the lab, and returning them.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of ex vivo gene therapy over in vivo?
o: Modified cells can be verified before reintroduction
gene_therapy_app.html.e: The ability to verify modified cells before reinfusion is the major safety advantage of ex vivo gene therapy.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: The first human gene therapy clinical trial (1990) targeted which disease?
gene_therapy_app.html.e: ADA-SCID (adenosine deaminase deficiency) was the target of the first approved human gene therapy trial in 1990.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: Which vector is most widely used in currently approved in vivo gene therapies?
gene_therapy_app.html.e: AAV (Adeno-Associated Virus) is the most popular and widely approved vector for in vivo gene therapy due to its safety profile.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: Suicide gene therapy in cancer works by:
o: Restoring the p53 tumour suppressor gene
Activating natural killer cells against tumours
Introducing a gene that converts a harmless prodrug into a toxic compound inside cancer cells
gene_therapy_app.html.e: Suicide gene therapy uses genes like HSV-TK; when given a prodrug, the enzyme produced by this gene converts it into a toxic compound that kills the cancer cell.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: CAR-T cell therapy is classified as which type of gene therapy?
gene_therapy_app.html.e: CAR-T is an ex vivo approach — T-cells are removed from the patient, engineered in the lab, and returned to target cancer cells.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: Insertional mutagenesis is a risk associated with which type of vector?
gene_therapy_app.html.e: Retroviral vectors integrate randomly into the host genome, risking activation of proto-oncogenes — a phenomenon called insertional mutagenesis.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: Which tumour suppressor gene is most commonly targeted in cancer gene therapy?
gene_therapy_app.html.e: p53 is the most important tumour suppressor targeted in cancer gene therapy; it is mutated in over 50% of human cancers.

gene_therapy_app.html.q: Germline gene therapy is considered controversial because:
o: Changes are heritable and can affect all future generations
It is less effective than somatic therapy
gene_therapy_app.html.e: Germline gene therapy modifies reproductive cells, meaning the genetic changes are permanent and passed to all future generations — raising serious ethical concerns.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: What is the primary purpose of CaCl₂ treatment in bacterial transformation?
o: To make bacteria competent by partially disrupting the outer membrane, allowing DNA uptake
To provide an energy source for DNA ligase
To select for transformed cells on agar plates
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: CaCl₂ treatment destabilises the outer membrane and cell wall of bacteria, making cells 'competent' — capable of binding and internalising exogenous DNA. The subsequent heat shock (42°C) drives the DNA through temporary membrane disruptions into the cell.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: Which gene transfer method is MOST efficient for stable in vivo gene delivery in animal cells?
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Transduction using viral vectors (especially AAV and lentiviral vectors) is the most efficient method for stable in vivo gene delivery. Viruses naturally evolved to efficiently infect cells and deliver their nucleic acids — efficiencies can exceed 90% in target cell types.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: In electroporation, how does DNA enter the cell?
o: DNA is injected mechanically through a glass needle
DNA is coated with cationic lipids and fuses with the cell membrane
A viral coat protein binds to a cell-surface receptor
A high-voltage electric pulse creates temporary pores in the plasma membrane through which DNA passes
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Electroporation uses a brief high-voltage electric pulse (0.1–10 kV/cm) to create temporary nanopores in the lipid bilayer. DNA enters through these transient pores by electrophoretic force and diffusion. Pores reseal spontaneously after the pulse.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: Liposome-mediated transfection (lipofection) delivers DNA into cells primarily via:
o: Direct injection using a microscope-guided needle
Endocytosis of lipoplexes followed by endosomal escape
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Cationic lipids form lipoplexes with DNA that bind the cell surface electrostatically. Cells internalise the lipoplexes by endocytosis. The fusogenic properties of the lipid components disrupt the endosomal membrane (endosomal escape), releasing DNA into the cytoplasm.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: Microinjection is primarily used to produce transgenic animals because it:
o: Delivers the highest efficiency of all methods
Is the only method that delivers DNA directly into the nucleus without any carrier
Can be performed on millions of cells simultaneously
Uses viral vectors which integrate into chromosomes
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Microinjection directly introduces DNA into the pronucleus of fertilised eggs using a glass needle guided by a micromanipulator. It requires no carrier, bypasses all cellular barriers, and delivers DNA directly to where integration can occur — making it ideal for transgenic animal production.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: Which viral vector integrates stably into the genome of NON-DIVIDING cells?
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Lentiviral vectors (derived from HIV) can integrate their genetic material into the genome of both dividing and non-dividing cells, because they encode a pre-integration complex that is actively transported into the nucleus. Classical retroviruses (MLV-based) require cell division for nuclear access.

o: Introduction of DNA into prokaryotic bacteria
Introduction of nucleic acids into eukaryotic cells by non-viral methods
Introduction of RNA into bacteria by heat shock
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Transfection specifically refers to the non-viral introduction of nucleic acids (DNA or RNA) into eukaryotic cells. It encompasses chemical methods (calcium phosphate, cationic lipids) and physical methods (electroporation, microinjection). The equivalent process in bacteria is called transformation.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) used in mRNA COVID-19 vaccines function primarily to:
o: Act as adjuvants to stimulate immune responses directly
Integrate the mRNA into the host genome
Protect fragile mRNA from nuclease degradation and enable its cellular uptake
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: LNPs encapsulate and protect the fragile mRNA from nuclease degradation in extracellular fluids, enable binding to cell surfaces and endocytic uptake, and facilitate endosomal escape to deliver intact mRNA into the cytoplasm for translation. mRNA does NOT integrate into the genome.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: A major advantage of transduction (viral gene delivery) over other methods is that it:
o: Can deliver very large DNA constructs of any size
Works only in rapidly dividing cells
Achieves the highest efficiency of gene delivery, especially in vivo
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Viral transduction achieves the highest efficiency of gene delivery, particularly in vivo. Viruses have evolved efficient mechanisms for cell entry via receptor-mediated infection. Efficiencies exceeding 90% in target cell types make transduction the gold standard for clinical gene therapy.

gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.q: Which of the following correctly pairs the gene transfer method with its primary characteristic?
o: Electroporation — electric pulse creates temporary membrane pores; works for bacteria and eukaryotes
Transformation — delivers DNA into eukaryotic cell nuclei by viral infection
Microinjection — uses electric pulses to create membrane pores for DNA entry
Liposome fusion — requires CaCl₂ and heat shock to make cells competent
gene_transfer_methods_rdna_host_cells.ht.e: Electroporation uses a high-voltage electric pulse to create temporary hydrophilic pores in the plasma membrane, and is applicable to both prokaryotic (bacteria) and eukaryotic cells. Transformation uses CaCl₂/heat shock for bacteria; microinjection uses mechanical injection; liposome fusion uses lipid vesicles.

hgp_ethics_ipr.html.q: The Human Genome Project was officially launched in:
hgp_ethics_ipr.html.e: The HGP began formally in 1990 and was completed in 2003.

hgp_ethics_ipr.html.q: The approximate number of protein-coding genes in the human genome is:
Craig Venter's Celera Genomics used the:
The unit of genetic (linkage) maps is:
hgp_ethics_ipr.html.e: Genetic distance is measured in centiMorgans.

hgp_ethics_ipr.html.q: ELSI in the HGP stands for:
The typical patent term under TRIPS is:

o: Deposit of micro-organisms for patent purposes
hgp_ethics_ipr.html.e: It recognises deposit of micro-organisms in patent procedure.

hgp_ethics_ipr.html.q: In India, which Section of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals and essentially biological processes?
Environmental release of GMOs in India is approved by:
The patent on turmeric's wound-healing use was revoked after a challenge by:
hgp_ethics_ipr.html.e: CSIR challenged the US patent in 1996; it was revoked in 1997.

hybridoma_monoclonal_antibodies.html.q: A hybridoma is a fusion of:
The myeloma cells used are deficient in:
hybridoma_monoclonal_antibodies.html.e: HGPRT-deficient cells cannot use the salvage pathway, so aminopterin kills them.

o: Blocks the de novo nucleotide synthesis pathway

hybridoma_monoclonal_antibodies.html.q: The chemical commonly used to fuse cells is:
Hybridoma culture supernatants are first screened by:
hybridoma_monoclonal_antibodies.html.e: ELISA detects antibody against the antigen.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: Which of the following is the most widely used microorganism for industrial ethanol production?
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's/brewer's yeast) is the preferred organism for ethanol production due to its high yield, ethanol tolerance (up to 14–15%), facultative anaerobic metabolism, and GRAS status.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: What is the net ATP yield from one molecule of glucose during anaerobic alcoholic fermentation?
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ Anaerobic fermentation yields only 2 ATP per glucose molecule (from glycolysis only). Aerobic respiration yields 36–38 ATP, but alcoholic fermentation is strictly anaerobic.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: The overall equation for alcoholic fermentation is:
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ The correct Gay-Lussac equation for alcoholic fermentation is: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + 2 ATP. This represents the conversion of one glucose into two ethanol molecules plus two CO₂ molecules.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: Which enzyme catalyses the conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde during alcoholic fermentation?
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ Pyruvate decarboxylase catalyses: Pyruvate → Acetaldehyde + CO₂. Then Alcohol dehydrogenase reduces acetaldehyde → Ethanol using NADH.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: What is the optimal temperature range for ethanol fermentation by Saccharomyces cerevisiae?
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ The optimal temperature for S. cerevisiae fermentation is 28–32°C. Below 20°C, metabolic rate drops significantly; above 40°C, enzymes are denatured and cells die.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: Molasses, used as a substrate in ethanol fermentation, is a by-product of:
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ Molasses is a thick, dark by-product of the sugar refining process (from sugarcane or sugar beet). It contains 45–55% fermentable sugars and is the cheapest widely used substrate for industrial ethanol production.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: Which of the following statements about the azeotrope of ethanol-water is CORRECT?
o: It is 95.6% ethanol and cannot be separated by simple distillation
It can be broken by adding more heat alone
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ The ethanol-water azeotrope contains 95.6% ethanol and 4.4% water. It boils at a constant temperature (78.2°C) and cannot be separated further by simple distillation. Molecular sieves or azeotropic distillation are used to produce anhydrous ethanol.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: What is the role of NAD⁺ regeneration in anaerobic fermentation?
o: It breaks down pyruvate into CO₂
It allows glycolysis to continue by accepting electrons from NADH
It activates the alcohol dehydrogenase enzyme
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ In the absence of oxygen, NAD⁺ must be regenerated from NADH so that glycolysis can continue. This is achieved by transferring electrons from NADH to acetaldehyde (producing ethanol), thereby regenerating NAD⁺.

industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.q: What is the typical ethanol concentration (% v/v) in fermented wash before distillation?
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ After fermentation, the fermented wash contains 8–12% v/v ethanol. This is because yeast is inhibited by higher ethanol concentrations (product inhibition above 14–15%). Distillation is required to concentrate it to 95–99%.

o: Increased fermentation in the presence of oxygen
Inhibition of fermentation by oxygen (aerobic respiration preferred)
The conversion of starch to glucose by amylase
The sterilisation of fermentation medium by heat
industrial_biotech_fermentation.html.e: ✅ The Pasteur Effect, described by Louis Pasteur, refers to the inhibition of fermentation by oxygen. When O₂ is available, yeast prefers aerobic respiration (higher ATP yield). Fermentation only dominates under anaerobic conditions.

molecular_markers_app.html.e: RFLP = Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism — DNA variation detected by differences in fragment lengths produced by restriction enzyme digestion.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: Which enzyme is central to the RFLP technique?
molecular_markers_app.html.e: Restriction endonucleases (restriction enzymes) cut DNA at specific palindromic recognition sequences, generating fragments of different lengths in different individuals.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: RAPD uses primers that are approximately how long?
molecular_markers_app.html.e: RAPD uses short arbitrary primers of approximately 10 nucleotides. Their short length and arbitrary sequence allow them to bind at multiple sites across the genome at low annealing temperature.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: RAPD is classified as a __________ marker.
molecular_markers_app.html.e: RAPD is a dominant marker — it detects the presence or absence of a band only. It cannot distinguish between homozygous (AA) and heterozygous (Aa) individuals, unlike co-dominant markers.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: DNA fingerprinting detects variation in which type of DNA sequences?
o: Variable Number Tandem Repeats (VNTRs) / Short Tandem Repeats (STRs)
molecular_markers_app.html.e: DNA fingerprinting exploits VNTRs (minisatellites) and STRs (microsatellites) — regions where short DNA sequences are repeated in tandem, with the number of repeats varying greatly between individuals.
Sir Alec Jeffreys at the University of Leicester, UK, developed DNA fingerprinting in 1984 and first applied it legally in 1986.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: Which step is unique to RFLP but NOT required in RAPD?
molecular_markers_app.html.e: Southern blotting and probe hybridisation are required in RFLP to detect specific fragments after gel separation. RAPD directly visualises PCR products on a gel — no Southern blotting is needed.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: Which molecular marker technique requires NO prior sequence knowledge of the genome?
molecular_markers_app.html.e: RAPD requires no prior DNA sequence knowledge — its arbitrary primers amplify random segments wherever they find complementary binding sites in the genome. This is its major practical advantage.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: In paternity testing using DNA fingerprinting, which principle applies?
o: Child's profile shares bands with both biological parents
Child's profile is identical to one parent
Child's profile is unrelated to parents
Child inherits all bands from the mother only
molecular_markers_app.html.e: Each child inherits approximately half its DNA from each biological parent. The child's DNA profile should therefore contain bands (alleles) shared with both the biological mother and biological father.

molecular_markers_app.html.q: Which of the following is NOT an application of DNA fingerprinting?
molecular_markers_app.html.e: Designing restriction enzymes is a protein engineering task unrelated to DNA fingerprinting. DNA fingerprinting applications include forensics, paternity testing, wildlife monitoring, individual identification, and population genetics.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: PCR was invented by whom and in which year?
pcr_principle_types_applications.html.e: PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction) was invented by Kary Mullis in 1983 while working at Cetus Corporation. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993 for this revolutionary invention. Sanger developed DNA sequencing in 1977; Watson and Crick described DNA structure in 1953.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: What is the correct sequence of the three stages of a PCR cycle?
pcr_principle_types_applications.html.e: The correct order is Denaturation (94–96°C) → Annealing (50–65°C) → Extension (72°C). First, DNA strands are separated by heat; then primers bind to their complementary sequences at lower temperature; finally, Taq polymerase extends the primers at 72°C to synthesise the new strand.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: What is the temperature used in the extension step of PCR and why?
o: 72°C — optimal temperature for Taq DNA polymerase activity
pcr_principle_types_applications.html.e: The extension step is performed at 72°C because this is the optimal activity temperature of Taq DNA polymerase (isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a hot spring bacterium). At 72°C, Taq extends primers at a rate of approximately 1000 bp/minute, synthesising the new complementary strand from the annealed primers.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: After 30 cycles of PCR starting from a single DNA molecule, approximately how many copies are produced?
pcr_principle_types_applications.html.e: The number of copies after n cycles = 2ⁿ. After 30 cycles: 2³⁰ = 1,073,741,824 ≈ 1 billion (10⁹) copies. This exponential amplification is the key power of PCR — each cycle doubles the number of copies, because products of each cycle serve as templates for the next.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: Which enzyme makes PCR practical for automation by withstanding repeated heating to 95°C?
pcr_principle_types_applications.html.e: Taq DNA Polymerase, isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, is heat-stable and survives the 94–96°C denaturation step that would destroy ordinary enzymes. Before Taq polymerase was used, researchers had to add fresh enzyme after each denaturation step, making automation impractical.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: In RT-PCR, what is the role of reverse transcriptase?
o: It denatures the DNA template at high temperature
It amplifies cDNA during thermal cycling
It labels the PCR product with fluorescence
It converts RNA (mRNA) into complementary DNA (cDNA) before PCR amplification
pcr_principle_types_applications.html.e: In RT-PCR, reverse transcriptase converts single-stranded mRNA into complementary DNA (cDNA) in a step BEFORE PCR thermal cycling. This reverse transcription step is essential because Taq polymerase can only copy DNA templates. The resulting cDNA then serves as the template for standard PCR amplification.

pcr_principle_types_applications.html.q: What is the main advantage of Nested PCR over conventional PCR?
o: It uses a lower denaturation temperature
It can amplify RNA directly without reverse transcription
It provides much higher sensitivity and specificity using two sets of primers
